item.title: Expanding the public transport network. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The government’s announcement to construct two monorail corridors across the capital by 2030 -- with BUET consultants completing pre-feasibility studies and detailed designs underway -- is certainly a welcome step in expanding Dhaka's public transportation network.
Designed to complement the existing Metro Rail and address last-mile connectivity in high-density bottlenecks, this appears a sensible undertaking to offer a viable, eco-friendly solution to chronic traffic gridlock that only seems to worsen in the capital.
Expanding mass transit has long been an absolute necessity for economic survival in the city, and it is good to see plans being developed to address it.
Yet, public enthusiasm for new transit infrastructure is inevitably tempered by a history of systemic mismanagement, and this apprehension is not without reason.
For decades, Bangladesh’s megaprojects have been plagued by a predictable blueprint of failure: Severe deadline extensions, rampant cost overruns, poor coordination, and opaque procurement processes that balloon into crushing public debts.
When major infrastructure ventures consistently double their original budgets, often as a result of incompetence, disregard, or simple administrative inertia, it is taxpayers who carry that unfair financial burden.
The proposed monorail initiative, and indeed subsequent infrastructure projects, must break decisively from this legacy of inefficiency. If this project suffers the same bureaucratic bloat and inflated expenditures that have tarnished past endeavours, its primary rationale will be completely compromised.
We must thus establish uncompromising governance from day one. The government must set firm, non-negotiable cost caps and strict timeline milestones, holding contractors and public officials accountable for any unjustified delays or financial leakages.
Building modern transit for Dhaka is a crucial step forward and has no alternative. However, it is doing it on time, within budget, and free of corruption that must be ensured.

item.title: There is no prosperity without women’s contribution. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:

Women entrepreneurs in particular can do so much more if given a level playing field. Tasking diplomatic missions with helping local women access global markets certainly points toward a visionary ambition, and we welcome it.
Yet, warm words and exhibition showcases will do nothing to alter economic realities unless the state backs them up with radical policy reform.
For decades, small and medium enterprises (SMEs), and particularly women-led businesses, have faced an unforgiving wall of bureaucratic red tape, institutional indifference, and severe financial exclusion.
The harsh reality is that women entrepreneurs across our nation do not merely need diplomatic exposure but need the very basics to operate a business - collateral-free credit, simplified bank loan processing, and protection from predatory lending.
Commercial banks continue to treat women-led SMEs as high-risk ventures, demanding unreasonable collateral and drowning applicants in paperwork. While state agencies draft grand blueprints for export expansion, countless grassroots creators struggle simply to open a basic merchant account or secure working capital.
From operationalizing dedicated, low-interest loan windows specifically tailored for women entrepreneurs to eliminating the bureaucratic hurdles to providing genuine training, digital literacy, and logistical backing for these women, these are just a few ways we can begin to include more women in our journey to economic prosperity.
A trillion-dollar economy cannot be built on the backs of marginalized innovators who are starved of capital and suffocated by red tape. We must move swiftly from policy speeches to concrete financial delivery.
If the government genuinely intends to harness women’s economic potential, structural support must replace empty promises.

item.title: Feeding children is just good economics. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Economics divides itself into two. Macroeconomics is about how the whole economy works, and it's what we always see the talking heads on TV chattering away about. Inflation, the deficit, interest rates, and so on. Macroeconomics is also the part of economics we don't know much about, and much of what we think we do is wrong.
Microeconomics is the details of prices and markets and interactions between people. Much of what we know here is correct even if many people would prefer that it weren't. For many people would much prefer it if humans didn't go around acting so human all the time.
Those words, macro and micro, also give us a clue. Macro means large, micro small. So, if you want to be a big and important person -- or a talking head on TV -- then you'll want to lean on macroeconomics. You know, chatter on about the big stuff.
But the bit that really makes the difference to how life is lived is that small stuff. As is true in life itself of course -- it's the little things that make life enjoyable and worth living. Further, with micro, we can do experiments and really zero in on what actually works.
The news is that the Bangladeshi government has understood one part of this sort of research and is even doing the right thing about it. It's this : “The government's school feeding initiative is set for a major expansion in 2027, with plans to increase coverage from 3.1 million to around 11 million students at government primary schools across the country.”
We could just say that parents should feed their kids at home and that's that. We could also say that isn't it great that the kids get a lovely meal from the government? But that's not really the point or issue here, it's this: “Ensuring student attendance.”
A lot of research has been done on who sends their kids to school and why. One alarming result was that when child labour is made illegal, then fewer poor children go to school. The logic is that some people are so really poor that any child has to start work so that that child brings in enough money to feed that very same child.
Poor parents know that education is a good thing, it will make the children richer when they're older. But it is necessary for that child to survive long enough to get older.
Research shows that such poor families might well send one or some of the children to school and others have to go to work in order to bring in the necessary money to feed all of them. Of course, it will be more likely to be girls who are made to work while the boys learn to read and write.
If we make child labour illegal, then this will lower the wages the children can receive when working. This is obvious and logical as people will exploit those working illegally more than those working legally. If the wages of the children working fall, more of the children have to work to be able to feed all of the children.
Note that economics is not saying this should happen. It's certainly not approving of it happening. It's just noting that this does happen.
We'd prefer there to be no child labour, of course we would. But as we see, just making it illegal can actually increase the amount of it.
So perhaps we require a different way of achieving our goal?
One of the basic findings of that whole field of microeconomics is that people respond to incentives. In fact, Charlie Munger (he was Warren Buffett's partner) used to say: “Show me the incentive and I'll tell you the outcome.”
Another way of putting that same point is that we should try to tempt people to do the right thing rather than attempt to force them. You know, promising a toddler a sweetie often works better than slapping them in getting them to do something.
So, to restate the poor children and school problem. The parents can only feed the child if the child works, so therefore the child doesn't go to school and is thus trapped in lifelong poverty.
What if we feed the child at school? Then they will both be fed and also be educated? And this time, all the kids can go to school because all the kids will be fed.
This has been studied a lot. There are whole shelves of research in libraries on this. As far as anyone can tell, this works really well.
The World Food Program from the Americans pays for this in many countries and is going to help in Bangladesh. There's also a charity, Mary's Meals, which does the same thing for whole countries. The charity does it possibly better and certainly cheaper than the government, but that's another story.
We've got something that is going to make that future world better. Children will be fed, that's good, but also more children will gain more education.
I personally don't like macroeconomics but a lot of that is because I simply cannot get my head around the advanced mathematics used in it. A failing of mine rather than the subject perhaps.
But I also like this microeconomics because it provides answers to how to make the world a better place in simple, pragmatic, doable ways.
We can just feed every child at school. Feeding every child at school works, makes the world a better place in the future. So, we should do that then.

item.title: What makes growth inclusive?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In recent times, there are renewed talks on the notion of inclusive growth. One question that keeps on popping up is what makes growth inclusive.
Everyone agrees that sustained economic growth is central to the ability of countries to advance human development and tackle poverty over a long period of time. But sustained growth alone is not enough to advance human development. For that, growth needs to be inclusive.
Inclusive growth is characterized by three mutually reinforcing elements:
Sustained growth which is pro-poor ensures poverty reduction as well as reduction in inequalities. Equity in resources, services, and income not only leads to human capabilities and opportunities, but it is also crucial for fair and just societies.
When growth is accompanied by rapid increases in productive employment, the incomes of and opportunities for the poor are likely to increase. Productive employment enhances livelihood, participation, dignity, and voice.
All together, inclusive growth is a driving force for human development and the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
To start with sustained growth is a prerequisite for inclusive growth. But sustained growth does not automatically become inclusive. In order to be inclusive, growth has to be pro-poor.
What is pro-poor growth?
The simplest notion of pro-poor growth assumes that so long as growth is associated with a reduction in poverty, it is pro-poor. The problem with this simple definition is that economic growth has largely been found to have some poverty-reducing impacts, at least through its trickledown effects. Thus, in terms of this simple definition, almost all economic growth is pro-poor.
The fundamental point, however, is that the “pro-poorness” of growth is not defined only by its poverty reduction impacts, but by the fact whether the poor actively engage in generating the growth, and also derive disproportionate benefits from it.
In other words, for growth to be pro-poor, the rate of income growth of the poor must exceed the rate of income growth of the non-poor and growth must accompanied by decreasing inequality.
While pro-poor growth is a necessary condition for inclusive growth, it is not a sufficient condition because it may not include non-poor people belonging to ethnic minorities, specific races, and so on. In many cases, these groups of people undertake economic activities which result in good livelihoods, but they have neither a voice in the decision-making process in the mainstream growth, nor are their activities integrated in it.
Equity remains at the heart of inclusive growth as distribution determines the pace, nature, and the pattern of growth. For growth to be inclusive, equity needs to be ensured on three planes:
If the production and the growth process start with an equitable distribution of assets, resources, and endowments, not only would they result in higher growth, but the benefits of growth are also equitably distributed.
When poor farmers have access to land and agricultural input packages, or small-scale entrepreneurs have access to credit, these not only enhance the growth process, but also ensure their fair share in it.
Infrastructure like roads, energy, transport, and communication has an economic activation effect, which implies new economic opportunities, better access to markets, and information. When poor people have access to such infrastructure, it makes growth pro-poor and inclusive.
Equitable access to basic social services, such as health and education and infrastructure, is another central factor for inclusive growth. The theoretical underpinning of this argument can be traced back to Amartya Sen’s work: Development as Freedom .
Inclusiveness effectively means eliminating the various “unfreedoms” experienced by individuals. According to Sen, people’s freedoms are enhanced through the provision of essential social services. Enhancing these freedoms is itself a precondition for achieving inclusive growth. An inclusive growth strategy, therefore, ensures that growth is promoted along with policies that enhance access to social services such as health and education.
In the realm of equity, redistribution of income is also associated with inclusive growth. This works on two fronts.
First , a redistribution of growth benefits the poor through enhancing their income, building their asset base, and enhancing their opportunities -- all of which ensure more inclusion of them in the growth process.
Second , a redistribution of income in various forms of social assistance to marginalized groups (eg, people with disabilities, older people), who cannot participate in the growth process, would provide social protection to them. These people are not part of the generation of growth but still become included in it as beneficiaries.
With regard to equity, two other observations may be pertinent in the context of inclusive growth.
First , equity is also a determining factor of the extent to which economic growth may impact poverty reduction. Initial inequality and changes in inequality are also important factors which can limit the extent to which poor people can participate in and benefit from growth.
Second , gender inequality impacts inclusive growth as well. Gender inequality in education and employment not only has a negative impact on economic growth, but it also adversely affects the pro-poorness of such growth. Also, significant gender gaps in access to agricultural productive assets and input such as land, fertilizer, and modern technologies seriously limit pro-poor growth.
Productive employment is a major driving force for inclusive growth. If growth is to be inclusive, it must be job-creating. This is because productive employment ensures people’s participation in the growth process, both as active agents as well as significant beneficiaries. And poor people can effectively be employed if economic growth is generated in sectors where they are concentrated and if labour-intensive technologies are used.
These linkages remind us of the importance of the sectoral composition of growth. The expansion of capital-intensive mining industries can result in jobless growth, making little impression on poverty. The incomes of the poor largely depend on the nature and extent of employment that economic growth generates.
It basically implies that not all growth is equally employment-intensive and there is no automatic link between economic growth and employment generation. Economic growth can be jobless, as the history of economic development has often shown.
Dr Selim Jahan is Former Director, Human Development Report Office and Poverty Division, United Nations Development Program, New York, USA.

The growing threat of unclean air. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dhaka's air pollution has once again reached alarming levels, with the capital recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 203 on Friday morning. Classified as “very unhealthy,” this reading is another reminder of a public health crisis that continues to receive far less attention than it deserves.
Air pollution is not a seasonal inconvenience that residents should simply learn to live with. It is a serious threat to public health, contributing to respiratory illnesses, cardiovascular diseases, and other long-term complications. Children, older people, and those with existing health conditions are particularly vulnerable, but the consequences extend to everyone who breathes the city's air.
The sources of this pollution are well known: Unregulated construction, road dust, emissions from ageing vehicles, industrial pollution, and brick kilns all contribute to the problem. Yet, despite repeated warnings and directives, meaningful improvements remain difficult to see.
The courts have previously issued directives to tackle air pollution, including controlling construction dust and shutting down illegal brick kilns. The continued deterioration of air quality raises serious questions about how effectively these measures are being enforced.
We need more than occasional drives and temporary interventions. Authorities must coordinate their efforts, enforce environmental regulations and hold those responsible for pollution accountable.
Construction sites must follow dust-control requirements, illegal brick kilns must be shut down, and vehicle emissions must be monitored more strictly. Regular monitoring and transparent reporting should also become standard practice.
At the same time, improving public transport, expanding green spaces, and investing in sustainable urban planning must be treated as long-term priorities.
People should not have to choose between going outside and protecting their health.
Let us be clear: Clean air is a basic necessity, not a privilege. Dhaka's worsening pollution demands urgent, sustained action. Another day of alarming AQI readings should not remain another day of inaction.

item.title: We need more public-private partnership. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A healthcare system under unrealistic pressure like ours needs practical ways to improve the quality and reach of public hospitals, and this initiative, if implemented carefully, could address some of the gaps that have long undermined public healthcare.
Under the proposed pilot, private partners will provide services at five tertiary-level hospitals, with fees still to be finalized before the program begins.
The intention to expand the model to other cities is also encouraging. Public hospitals face shortages of equipment, specialized services, and trained personnel. Private expertise and investment could improve facilities, strengthen management, and give patients access to treatment that might otherwise be out of reach.
However, this partnership must strengthen public healthcare, not make essential treatment a privilege. Fees charged by private partners need to be reasonable and clearly disclosed. Patients should not face unexpected costs, and those unable to afford additional charges must not be pushed aside.
The government must set firm standards for service quality, monitor performance, and hold partners accountable for meeting agreed targets.
The initiative must also complement sustained public investment. Bangladesh cannot rely on private participation alone to resolve long standing weaknesses in healthcare.
Hospitals need adequate staffing, functioning equipment, regular maintenance and better management. Plans to recruit more doctors and expand critical care facilities must move forward without unnecessary delays.
The five-hospital pilot should be an opportunity to measure results and correct shortcomings before expansion. The government must publish clear information on costs, services and outcomes so the public can judge whether the program is working.
This is precisely the kind of practical initiative the health sector needs more of. With transparency, affordability, and proper oversight, partnerships can help deliver better care to more people.
The real test, however, will be whether patients experience meaningful improvements.

item.title: Men neither see nor listen to women. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Searching the Dhaka Tribune last week for a piece of my own, I came instead upon an essay I have not been able to put down: Shuchi binte Shahjalal’s The women are divine .
She opens with the old belief of the idol-makers: That a Durga is incomplete unless a little earth from a sex worker’s doorstep is worked into her clay -- for a man leaves his virtue at that threshold, and the ground there turns holy. The goddess cannot be finished without the woman’s soil; the woman herself cannot be let into the festival. The earth is holy, she writes. The person is not.
Let me say at once what I am and am not doing. I am a man, and this is a piece about men. I will not presume to explain to the women of my homeland a cage they have mapped, from the inside, far better than I can.
Shuchi has already said the essential thing, with a scholar’s range and a poet’s aim. I want only to add a footnote -- from the poet we Bengalis reach for whenever we wish to sound reverent about women, and whom, I have come to think, we never actually heard.
We are fond of Tagore as a worshipper of the feminine. We quote him at weddings and drape our daughters’ recitals in his songs. It is worth remembering, then, that at his most attentive, the Bishwakobi was not building the pedestal Shuchi describes. He was warning against it.
I have spent this autumn translating his love songs, one line at a time, and two of them will not now leave me.
The first is Bhalobeshe, sokhi, nibhrite jatone -- “Love me, and in the quiet shrine of your heart, write my name.” Midway, the lover makes a stranger, smaller request:
“Keep, with tender care, my chattering bird, in the courtyard of your palace.”
Read it slowly, and the bird is no ornament. The whole ache of the song is the plea that it be kept, tended, listened to.
In a second song, Tumi ki keboli chhobi -- “Are you only a picture?” -- he almost begs her not to harden into mere paint on a canvas, to be real and present, not an image he can hang on a wall and admire.
A century before our present arguments, Tagore had already named the two ways a man fails a woman: He stops listening to her voice, and he lets her freeze into an image.
Shuchi calls on Nazrul, who dared to address the barangana , the prostitute, as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her.
Let me call on the other giant, who stands, I think, exactly where she does -- on the side of the woman no one will look at or listen to.
Her essay is unsparing about what reverence costs, in life and in death. She recalls the roughly 1,500 women driven from the Kandapara brothel in Tangail in 2014, long after a High Court had ruled such evictions unconstitutional; the sex workers ridiculed when they report rape, because the society “cannot imagine a sex worker being raped”; and Hamida Begum, who in 2020 became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a proper Islamic burial -- after which the imam who prayed over her said he would not do it again, having been scolded by his neighbours.
Beside these, she sets the national figures she cites: By the counts of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, 786 women and girls raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before; and almost 22,000 cases of violence against women and children logged by police in a single year.
I will not borrow her numbers to decorate an argument of my own. I note only what she notices -- that behind each is a woman whom a society that sorts its women into goddesses and fallen women has filed under the second heading.
And I would underline, for every man who thinks himself devout, the sentence of hers that ought to be read aloud from pulpits: A society that calls its women mothers and then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist walks, has not forgotten reverence -- it has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
Here, let me add the one thing a lifetime in medicine has taught me, because it bears on her point that rape is treated as a stain on a woman’s honour rather than a crime against her body.
I have spent my working life with the human heart -- the actual muscle, four chambers, no holier in a saint than in a so-called fallen woman. A body keeps no ledger of honour. It bleeds the same, grieves the same, heals or fails to heal the same, whatever box the neighbours have assigned its owner.
When we treat a woman’s injury as a stain on her family’s ijjat rather than harm to her person, we are not being moral. We are staring at the honour and refusing to see the woman -- the same failure, once more.
So the answer, I think, is not less reverence but reverence that finally opens its eyes. Read generously, the idol-maker’s belief is almost holy: The goddess is made, in part, of the outcast woman’s earth; the divine and the discarded are the same clay.
The tragedy is only that we stop at the clay. We bow to the figure and walk past the person who gave it her soil.
Tagore points where Shuchi points. Keep the chattering bird -- do not cage it, do not silence it, bend down and listen. Do not let her become only a picture on the wall.
The cure for a goddess no one can bear to meet is not to break her into a “fallen” woman; it is to come down off our own certainty and stand beside her at the doorstep -- to see her face, and to hear her voice.
Shuchi binte Shahjalal has written the diagnosis. The least her countrymen -- and I mean the men -- can do is read it with our eyes open for once, and admit what it took a woman on the Op-Ed desk to say plainly.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, many still hiding their faces: Divine in theory, and in practice neither seen nor heard.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, where he practises medicine.

item.title: Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: Lost in translation? Japanese minister blames X for diplomatic embarrassment. [ dawn ]
item.description:
TOKYO: A Japanese minister blamed Elon Musk’s X social media platform on Friday for almost plunging him into diplomatic hot water, after its automatic translation feature implied he did not know the names of world leaders he was meeting.

Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa assured reporters that he knew the identity of the current prime minister of Bangladesh after a post with photos of the two included the name of ousted premier Sheikh Hasina in its translated version.

“This is actually a serious matter. It is possible that the Bangladeshi public might be left with the impression that, Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry does not even know who our (Bangladeshi) prime minister is,” Akazawa told journalists.

His original Japanese-language post on X on Oct 28, accompanied by photos, stated that he met visiting Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

But the platform’s machine-translation tool incorrectly changed the English version to make Akazawa seem to declare that he met Sheikh Hasina, who has lived in exile in India since an uprising in 2024.

Making matters worse, it was not the first time Akazawa had fallen foul of a translation snafu on the platform.

He said a similar mistake occurred after he posted about his online meeting with Kuwait’s Oil Minister Tareq Al-Roumi on Thursday -- with the automatic translation feature saying he held talks with Qatar’s energy minister.

Akazawa added that his translated post on a meeting with US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also stated an incorrect name.

“I experienced this three times,” he said, appealing to X to fix the translation tool.

Published in Dawn, November 7th, 2026
